\[

Usually, for the equation $\partial_t u = \Delta_p(u^q)$, one looks at the behavior of solutions.
Let $w = u^q$. Then $u = w^{1/q}$.
$\nabla u = \frac{1}{q} w^{1/q - 1} \nabla w$.
$|\nabla u|^p = \frac{1}{q^p} w^{p(1/q - 1)} |\nabla w|^p = \frac{1}{q^p} w^{p/q - p} |\nabla w|^p$.
The equation for $w$ is roughly $\partial_t w = \Delta_p w + \text{lower order terms}$.
Actually, the equation is $\partial_t u = \text{div}(|\nabla u^q|^{p-2} \nabla(u^q))$.
Let $v = u^q$. Then $\nabla v = q u^{q-1} \nabla u$. So $|\nabla u| = \frac{1}{q} u^{1-q} |\nabla v| = \frac{1}{q} v^{(1-q)/q} |\nabla v|$.
Then $|\nabla u|^p = \frac{1}{q^p} v^{\frac{p}{q}(1-q)} |\nabla v|^p$.
The term inside the divergence is $|\nabla v|^{p-2} \nabla v$, which is the standard $p$-Laplacian part applied to $v$.
So the equation for $v$ is $\partial_t (v^{1/q}) = \Delta_p v$.
